# saebenchmarking

<!-- badges: start -->

[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/fionaaudia/saebenchmarking/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/fionaaudia/saebenchmarking/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

## Overview

saebenchmarking provides model-agnostic **difference**, **ratio**, and
**optimum** benchmarking for small area estimators, together with mean
squared error (MSE) estimation, so that weighted small area aggregates
are consistent with a known external or internal target.

Point estimation methods follow You & Rao (2002), Wang, Fuller & Qu
(2008), and Rao & Molina (2015, Section 6.4.6). MSE estimation follows
Butar & Lahiri (2003) and Steorts & Ghosh (2013) for a residual
bootstrap approach, and Datta, Ghosh, Steorts & Maples (2011) for a
posterior-simulation approach suited to Hierarchical Bayes estimators.

## Installation

You can install the development version of saebenchmarking from
[GitHub](https://github.com/) with:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("fionaaudia/saebenchmarking")
```

## Example

### Difference benchmarking

This is a basic example showing how to benchmark small area estimates so
that their weighted aggregate matches a known external target.

``` r
library(saebenchmarking)

est    <- c(10.2, 8.7, 12.1)
mse    <- c(0.5, 0.4, 0.6)
weight <- c(0.3, 0.4, 0.3)

hasil <- sae_benchmarking(
  method   = "difference",
  estimate = est,
  mse      = mse,
  weight   = weight,
  target   = 10
)

hasil$benchmark$estimation
#>        Estimation
#> Area_1      10.03
#> Area_2       8.53
#> Area_3      11.93
hasil$aggregation
#>                          Y
#> Aggregation_Direct      NA
#> Aggregation_Bench    10.00
#> Aggregation_Estimate 10.17
#> Target               10.00
```

### Ratio and optimum benchmarking

The same call works with `method = "ratio"` or `method = "optimum"`;
only the internal adjustment differs.

``` r
sae_benchmarking(
  method   = "ratio",
  estimate = est,
  mse      = mse,
  weight   = weight,
  target   = 10
)$benchmark$estimation
#>        Estimation
#> Area_1  10.029499
#> Area_2   8.554572
#> Area_3  11.897738

sae_benchmarking(
  method   = "optimum",
  estimate = est,
  mse      = mse,
  weight   = weight,
  target   = 10
)$benchmark$estimation
#>        Estimation
#> Area_1  10.043558
#> Area_2   8.533129
#> Area_3  11.912270
```

### Internal benchmarking (no external target)

If you don’t have an external target, supply `direct` estimates instead
and the target is computed internally as their weighted sum.

``` r
direct <- c(10.5, 8.2, 12.8)
vardir <- c(0.6, 0.5, 0.7)

hasil_internal <- sae_benchmarking(
  method   = "difference",
  estimate = est,
  mse      = mse,
  weight   = weight,
  direct   = direct,
  vardir   = vardir
)

hasil_internal$benchmark$target
#> [1] 10.27
```

### Estimating the MSE of benchmarked estimates

`mse_benchmarking()` takes the output of `sae_benchmarking()` and
estimates the MSE of the *benchmarked* estimates. When `direct` and
`vardir` are available, it uses a residual bootstrap by default:

``` r
mse_benchmarking(hasil_internal, B = 200, seed = 1)
#> $method
#> [1] "difference"
#> 
#> $approach
#> [1] "bootstrap"
#> 
#> $MSE
#>              MSE
#> Area_1 0.6476198
#> Area_2 0.4878425
#> Area_3 0.7651982
#> 
#> $B
#> [1] 200
#> 
#> $n_failed
#> [1] 0
```

For Hierarchical Bayes estimators, supply a matrix of posterior draws
instead, and the posterior-simulation approach is used:

``` r
set.seed(1)
posterior_draws <- matrix(
  rnorm(300 * 3, rep(est, each = 300), sqrt(mse)),
  ncol = 3
)

mse_benchmarking(hasil, posterior_samples = posterior_draws)
#> $method
#> [1] "difference"
#> 
#> $approach
#> [1] "posterior"
#> 
#> $Estimation
#>        Estimation
#> Area_1  10.057941
#> Area_2   8.530774
#> Area_3  11.901027
#> 
#> $MSE
#>              MSE
#> Area_1 0.3652560
#> Area_2 0.2850895
#> Area_3 0.4025422
```
